To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the interrupted torsion test can be used for simulating rolling of round bar made from steel 32CrBs4 with the fi nal microstructures with coarser grains.
the compression tests at 900°C and 850°C with the controlled cooling to 200°C are the most appropriate to simulate the laboratory rolling of round bars made of the steel 32CrBs.
the compression test at the temperature of the end cooling of 300 °C is the most suitable plastometric method for simulation of hot rolling in the case of the steel 32CrBs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of the applicability of the various plastometric methods for the simulation of hot rolling.
the comparison of the results of the compression tests and the interrupted torsion test, which is an alternative to the compression test, in the simulation of hot rolling.
the comparison of various methods for simulating rolling of steel bars, which are based on the plastometric method.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the interrupted torsion test is more reliable for the prediction of the hot rolling parameters than the compression test.
the compression test is more sensitive to the temperature of the fi nal stage of cooling than the torsion test.
the compression test is more suitable for simulation of the hot rolling process than the interrupted torsion test.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the results obtained by the interrupted torsion test are closer to the results of physical simulation of hot rolling than the results of compression test.
both types of tests can be used for the simulation of rolling of the investigated material, but the compression test is more suitable for this purpose than the interrupted torsion test.
the interrupted torsion tests and compression tests with controlled cooling are suitable for simulation of the hot rolling of the round steel bar.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the results of simulation tests can be used for the prediction of the microstructure and mechanical properties of the material after the hot rolling process only in case that the cooling rate of samples after the tests is similar to the cooling rate in the real process.
the results of compression tests with controlled cooling of the sample after the deformation are closer to the results of laboratory rolling.
the compression test can be successfully applied in the simulation of hot rolling, provided that the temperature of the end cooling is properly chosen.
